content_voiceover: This slide shows the classic clinical spectrum of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, also called Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, an autosomal dominant vascular disorder. Panels A and B show mucocutaneous telangiectasias, small blanching red spots on the lip, tongue, and fingertips, which are the most visible and earliest clue on exam. But the boards-relevant danger is visceral involvement, shown in panels C and D. Panel C is a chest x-ray and panel D is a pulmonary angiogram demonstrating a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, a direct right-to-left shunt between a pulmonary artery and vein that bypasses the capillary bed. These pulmonary AVMs matter enormously because they create a paradoxical embolism risk, meaning clots or even bacteria can cross straight to the systemic circulation and cause stroke or brain abscess without ever passing through the lung filter. HHT patients also commonly have GI telangiectasias causing occult bleeding and iron deficiency anemia, plus hepatic AVMs. So the pattern to remember is mucocutaneous telangiectasias plus recurrent epistaxis plus visceral AVMs, especially pulmonary, hepatic, and cerebral.
keypoints: Mucocutaneous telangiectasias: lips, tongue, fingertips (A, B)
Pulmonary AVM → paradoxical embolism → stroke, brain abscess
Also screen for hepatic and GI AVMs/telangiectasias
keypoint_voiceover: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, or Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome, is autosomal dominant. Look for mucocutaneous telangiectasias on the lips, tongue, and fingertips. The dangerous finding is a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, a right-to-left shunt seen here on chest x-ray and pulmonary angiogram. Because blood bypasses the capillary filter, pulmonary AVMs carry a paradoxical embolism risk, leading to stroke or brain abscess. Also remember to screen these patients for hepatic and gastrointestinal AVMs.
